meaning: The same verb is repeated to show an action done over and over, to the extreme: "... and ... again," "... with all one's might."
connection: Verb masu-stem + に + same verb in te-form / ta-form

senses.label: ... over and over
senses.meaning: 「〜に〜て」 links to the next clause. It stresses a long, thorough process that leads to the result. Common: 「考えに考えて」, 「悩みに悩んで」, 「迷いに迷って」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + に + same verb te-form (考えに考えて, 走りに走って)
examples: After thinking it over and over, I decided to quit my job.
This is a conclusion I reached after agonizing over it.
I ran and ran all the way to the station and just made the last train.

senses.label: Extremely ...
senses.meaning: 「〜に〜た」 ends a sentence or modifies a noun to show an extreme degree. 「待ちに待った」 ("long-awaited") is a set phrase.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + に + same verb ta-form (待ちに待った + noun, 泣きに泣いた)
examples: The long-awaited summer vacation has arrived.
That night, she cried and cried.
The carefully refined proposal was finally accepted.

notes: The verb before and after 「に」must be the same: ✕「考えに悩んで」→ ○「考えに考えて」「悩みに悩んで」.
Don't confuse it with the purpose 「に」: 「買いに行った」means "went to buy" (two different verbs), while 「買いに買った」means "bought and bought."
It works only with actions or states that can continue or repeat. Instantaneous verbs like 「死ぬ」and 「着く」normally don't take it: 「死にに死んだ」and 「着きに着いた」sound wrong.
It narrates an experience with a note of feeling, so it isn't used for commands or requests: ✕「考えに考えてください」→ ○「よく考えてください」.

daily.title: The big day arrives
daily.description: A child's long-awaited trip is finally here.
daily.example: The long-awaited day of our trip has finally come!

daily.title: Explaining your choice
daily.description: Telling a friend you decided after a lot of hesitation.
daily.example: I went back and forth for ages and finally chose this university.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A scene of a character in deep grief.
daily.example: The boy who had lost his mother cried and cried all night.

work.title: Product launch
work.description: The person in charge presents a carefully polished new product.
work.example: Let me introduce a new product our development team has refined again and again.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on negotiations that dragged on.
work.example: After a long and bitter dispute, the negotiations finally reached an agreement.

etymology: 「に」 originally marked purpose or addition: "in order to ..." or "on top of ...". Stacking the same verb means adding the same action again and again, which gives the sense of "repeatedly, to the extreme."

similar.title: 〜に〜を重ねて
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express repetition and accumulation. 「〜に〜を重ねて」repeats a noun (「努力に努力を重ねて」) and is more bookish. 「〜に〜て」repeats a verb (「考えに考えて」) and has more emotional colour.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「考え抜く」stresses seeing it through to the end, thoroughly. 「考えに考える」stresses how many times and how hard the process was, with stronger feeling.

similar.title: 〜に〜に (listing)
similar.explanation: Related (both use the additive 「に」). 「〜に〜に」links different nouns to list them, "this and that and ...". 「〜に〜て」links the same verb to show one action repeated.

formation: The pattern is verb masu-stem + 「に」+ the same verb. The masu-stem can act as a noun (考え = "thought"), and 「に」expresses addition, the same 「に」as in 「AにBを加える」("add B to A"). So 「考えに考える」is "thinking piled on top of thinking." Stacking the same action layer upon layer naturally gives the sense of repeated, thorough, to-the-limit effort. With the te-form leading into the next clause, it stresses "after all that, this was the result"; with the ta-form (「待ちに待った」), the accumulated degree is exclaimed as the result itself.

meaning: Uses 「に」 to pile up items one after another: "A, B, and C too," stressing that there are many things.

senses.label: One thing after another
senses.meaning: Lists tasks you're juggling at once, stressing how busy you are. Common: 「〜に〜にと忙しい」, 「〜に〜に追われる」.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun + にと + 忙しい／追われる
examples: Between studying and club activities, I lead a busy life.
Between work, housework, and childcare, I have no time for myself.

senses.label: Item after item
senses.meaning: Adds items one by one: "A, plus B, plus C." Often used for food or things that go together.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun + に + noun
examples: Beer, edamame, and yakitori: there's no greater happiness.
The table was lined with treats like sushi and tempura.

notes: It connects nouns only, never verbs: ✕「掃除するに洗濯するにと忙しい」→ ○「掃除に洗濯にと忙しい」.
It stresses "one thing after another, lots of them." To simply and objectively pair two items, use 「と」: ✕「東京に大阪に行った」→ ○「東京と大阪に行った」.
When describing how busy you are, 「と」normally follows the last item before the predicate (「〜に〜にと忙しい」). Dropping 「と」and going straight to 「忙しい」sounds unnatural.

daily.title: Talking about student life
daily.description: A college student tells a relative how things are going.
daily.example: Between classes, my part-time job, and my club, I'm rushing around every day.

daily.title: Ordering at a get-together
daily.description: A friend excitedly orders a pile of dishes at an izakaya.
daily.example: Fried chicken, fries, sashimi: let's just order it all.

work.title: Employee interview
work.description: A working mom talks about balancing work and family in the company newsletter.
work.example: Between work and raising kids, every day is one challenge after another.

etymology: 「に」 has a sense of "adding" (as in 「AにBを加える」). Linking nouns with 「に」 one after another produces the listing meaning "and on top of that ...".

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Both list things. 「〜や〜など」just gives a few examples in a neutral tone. 「〜に〜に」stresses piling up one item after another, highlighting "many, busy, complete."

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: Both can list a flurry of things. 「〜やら〜やら」often has a negative feel of "a jumble, more than I can handle." 「〜に〜に」can also be used in positive contexts (「ごちそう」).

similar.title: 〜だの〜だの
similar.explanation: Both list things. 「〜だの〜だの」is mostly used to list someone's complaints or demands, with a tone of dissatisfaction. 「〜に〜に」has no such negative colour.

formation: 「に」originally means addition (「AにBを加える」, 「鬼に金棒」). A noun followed by 「に」and then the next noun amounts to "A, and on top of that B," piling items up one by one. So it isn't a flat list: it gives a feeling of "more and more," which is why it suits busyness (「勉強に部活に」) or abundance (「ビールに枝豆に」). The final 「と」wraps up the list and leads into a predicate such as 「忙しい」.

meaning: 「一〜や二〜」 means "just one or two," stressing a small number that is nothing unusual or not worth worrying about.
connection: 一 + counter + や + 二 + counter (一度や二度, 一人や二人)

senses.label: Just one or two
senses.meaning: "One or two is normal, nothing special." Often followed by 「は（誰にでも）ある」 or 「くらい」. Used to comfort or show tolerance.
senses.connection: Noun の + 一つや二つ／一度や二度 + は
examples: Everyone fails once or twice.
It's only natural to have a flaw or two.
You'll make a friend or two in no time.

senses.label: More than once or twice
senses.meaning: With the negative 「〜ではない」, it means "far more than once or twice," stressing how often. Often carries frustration or emotion.
senses.connection: 一度や二度／一回や二回 + ではない
examples: This isn't the first or second time he's been late.
We've had this kind of complaint many more times than once or twice.

senses.label: Even that much is fine
senses.meaning: "That small amount is nothing." Followed by "it's fine," "I don't mind," and so on.
senses.connection: 一日や二日／一万円や二万円 + ても／くらい
examples: I'm fine even if I don't sleep for a day or two.
If it's ten or twenty thousand yen, I'll lend it to you.

notes: Affirmative and negative mean opposite things: 「一度や二度はある」= "once or twice is normal (few)"; 「一度や二度ではない」= "far more than once or twice (many)." Overlook 「ではない」and the meaning flips.

If you made the mistake yourself, saying 「ミスの一つや二つ、誰にでもあります」to a client will be taken as downplaying it and shifting blame, which is very rude. This kind of tolerant remark can only come from the other party or a bystander.
The counters must match: ✕「一人や二つ」→ ○「一人や二人」. The pair is fixed as "one" and "two"; 「一度や三度」doesn't work.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Your friend is down after failing an exam.
daily.example: Don't get discouraged over failing once or twice.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A wife is fed up with her husband forgetting things.
daily.example: This isn't the first time you've forgotten a promise, is it?

work.title: A boss encouraging a new hire
work.description: A boss talks to a new employee who made a mistake.
work.example: Don't worry about a mistake or two.

work.title: Customer complaint meeting
work.description: The person in charge stresses that the problem isn't a one-off.
work.example: We have received similar complaints more than just once or twice.

etymology: 「や」 is a listing particle. Pairing the two smallest numbers, 「一」 and 「二」, means "a tiny amount like one or two," which leads to the nuance "nothing unusual, not worth mentioning."

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (belittling / minimum)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can express "the bare minimum, no big deal." 「一度くらい」gives only one number and can be used in requests (「一度くらい行ってみたい」). 「一度や二度」pairs two numbers and carries a more tolerant "nothing unusual, happens to everyone" tone.

similar.title: 〜たりとも
similar.explanation: Both use a minimal quantity such as "one" for emphasis. 「一円たりとも」stresses "not even one, not allowed," is followed by a negative, and sounds stern. 「一つや二つ」stresses "one or two is fine, perfectly normal."

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Related (both use the listing particle 「や」). 「〜や〜など」is ordinary example-listing. This entry is the fixed pattern 「一〜や二〜」, used specifically for small amounts.

formation: It is 「一〜」+ the listing particle 「や」+ 「二〜」. 「や」lists some items without exhausting the set, and using the two smallest numbers, "one" and "two," amounts to saying "a small number like one or two." Small number → "not worth mentioning, happens to anyone," which brings a tolerant, consoling tone. Followed by the negative 「ではない」, it means "far more than one or two," stressing a large amount. A 「noun + の」often comes first (「失敗の一度や二度」) to specify what the "one or two" are.

meaning: Attaches to the verb masu-stem to make a noun meaning the "way something looks / its degree" or the "way of doing something."

senses.label: The way someone looks
senses.meaning: Shows how a state shows itself and to what degree, usually a strong emotion or reaction. Common: 「〜ようといったら」, 「大変な〜ようだ」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + よう (喜びよう, 慌てよう, 落ち込みよう)
examples: You should have seen how happy he was when he found out he passed.
She was so depressed it was painful to watch.
Seeing how angry my father was, I realized how serious it was.

senses.label: The way of doing
senses.meaning: Shows a method or way. Common: 「ものは言いようだ」 ("it's all in how you say it"), 「考えようによっては」 ("depending on how you look at it"), 「やりようはある」 ("there's always a way").
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + よう + は／によって（は）／だ (言いよう, 考えよう, やりよう)
examples: It's all in how you say it; the way you phrase things changes how others take it.
Depending on how you look at it, this failure is also a good experience.
Even without time, there are plenty of ways to do it.

notes: It must attach to the masu-stem: ✕「喜ぶようといったら」→ ○「喜びようといったら」. 「喜ぶようだ」, with the plain form, means "seems pleased," which is a completely different meaning.

Don't confuse it with the volitional: 「考えようによっては」means "depending on how you look at it," while a bare 「考えよう」at the end of a sentence means "let's think." Check whether it's followed by 「は」, 「によって」, 「といったら」and the like.
「ものは言いようだ」implies "you can make anything sound good by rewording it." Using it to comment on what someone said hints that they're making excuses, so it's rude to say to a boss or client.

daily.title: Describing a family member's reaction
daily.description: Telling a friend how your child reacted to a present.
daily.example: Seeing how happy my son was, I was glad I bought it.

daily.title: Telling a friend to lighten up
daily.description: A friend frets over something small, and you suggest another angle.
daily.example: Well, it all depends on how you look at it.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character is described panicking.
daily.example: From how flustered he was, it was clear he was hiding something.

work.title: Discussing solutions
work.description: A project hits trouble, and a senior colleague encourages the team.
work.example: Even with a small budget, there must be a way.

work.title: A reminder about wording
work.description: A boss reminds a team member to watch their wording when replying to a client.
work.example: Even the same content can cause friction depending on how you say it.

etymology: 「よう」 is written 「様」 and originally means "appearance, form." After a verb's continuative form (masu-stem), it means "how the action looks," and by extension "the way of doing it."

similar.title: 〜方（かた）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can express a way of doing something. 「読み方」is an objective method or procedure. 「読みよう」leans toward "how you take or handle it," often implying that different approaches give different results.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: Related. 「〜ようがない」is the negative idiom of the "method" sense, meaning "there's no way to ..." (「連絡の取りようがない」). This entry is the affirmative or neutral "manner, way."

similar.title: 〜ようによっては
similar.explanation: Related. 「〜ようによっては」is a fixed collocation of the "method" sense meaning "depending on how you ..." (「考えようによっては」). This entry also covers manner and degree, as in 「喜びよう」.

similar.title: 〜ぶり・〜ぶりに
similar.explanation: Both can describe a manner. 「仕事ぶり」and 「話しぶり」objectively describe the state or style of an action. When 「〜よう」describes a manner, it puts more weight on the extent (「喜びようといったら」).

formation: 「よう」is 「様」, originally "appearance, manner." The masu-stem works like a noun, so adding 「様」makes it "the manner of this action": 「喜びよう」= "the way someone is pleased." The "manner" of an action can be understood as the degree it shows (「喜びようといったら」= "incredibly pleased") or as "how to do it," that is, the method (「言いよう」, 「やりよう」). Add a negative to the latter and you get 「〜ようがない」("no way to do it" → "can't"), showing that all these uses come from the same 「様」.

meaning: Adds 「も」 to the verb masu-stem and negates it, stressing "not even (this basic thing)." Often shows annoyance, surprise, or the unexpected.
connection: Verb masu-stem + もしない／もしなかった

senses.label: Not even ...
senses.meaning: Stresses that someone doesn't do even the most basic action. Usually shows the speaker's annoyance or blame. Common: 「見向きもしない」, 「振り向きもしない」, 「読みもしない」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + もしない (見向きもしない, 返事もしない, 見もしない)
examples: He won't even pay attention to what I say.
He threw away the letter I worked so hard on without even reading it.
Even when I called him, my son didn't so much as turn around.

senses.label: Never even imagined
senses.meaning: 「思いもしなかった」, 「考えもしなかった」, 「予想もしなかった」 mean something was completely unexpected. The tone is surprise, not blame.
senses.connection: 思い／考え／予想 + もしなかった
examples: I never dreamed I'd actually win.
I never imagined it would turn out like this.

senses.label: Nonexistent
senses.meaning: 「ありもしない」 and 「できもしない」 modify nouns: "that doesn't exist at all / that can't be done at all." Used to criticize made-up stories or empty promises.
senses.connection: ありもしない／できもしない + noun
examples: I'm troubled because someone is spreading groundless rumors about me.
You shouldn't make promises you can't keep.

notes: It carries strong reproach. Using 「読みもしない」or 「返事もしない」about a boss or client is very rude; it suits only complaining to friends or describing a third party.
「思いもしなかった」and 「予想もしなかった」express surprise, "never imagined," not reproach. Don't read them as "didn't even want to think about it."
The verb takes the masu-stem: ✕「見るもしない」→ ○「見もしない」. For suru-verbs, say 「勉強もしない」(noun + 「も」).
Don't confuse it with 「何もしない」or 「誰もしない」: a question word + 「も」is total negation ("does nothing"), without the sense of "not even the bare minimum."

daily.title: Complaining about a child
daily.description: Mom complains her kid ignored the meal she worked hard on.
daily.example: I went to the trouble of cooking, and he left without even eating.

daily.title: Telling a friend about a surprise
daily.description: A friend throws you a surprise birthday party.
daily.example: I never imagined a surprise like this!

daily.title: When falsely accused
daily.description: Misunderstood by a classmate, you vent to a friend.
daily.example: I can't believe I'm being blamed for something I didn't even do.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report says executives ignored a problem.
work.example: The management didn't even listen to the employees' complaints.

work.title: Project review
work.description: Explaining an unexpected problem at a post-mortem.
work.example: No one anticipated this kind of trouble.

etymology: Built from verb masu-stem (continuative form) + the particle 「も」 + 「しない」. Here 「も」 means "even," singling out the action itself and negating it, which creates the emphasis "not even the most basic thing."

similar.title: 〜もしないで
similar.explanation: Related. 「〜もしないで」is followed by another action (「読みもしないで捨てた」), meaning "without even ... did ...". 「〜もしない」ends the sentence or modifies a noun.

similar.title: 〜やしない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both strengthen the negative. 「〜やしない」means "not at all" and is more colloquial and blunter. 「〜もしない」adds a layer of "not even," stressing that even the bare minimum wasn't done.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「見さえしない」and 「見もしない」both mean "doesn't even look," but 「さえ」stresses "this is the most extreme example," so it sounds heavier.

formation: The structure is verb masu-stem (nominalized) + 「も」+ 「しない」. The action is first turned into a noun, then the negative of 「する」denies it outright, and the 「も」in between means "even." The speaker treats the action as "the very least one should do," and denying even that produces dissatisfaction or surprise: "doesn't even ...". 「ありもしない」has the same structure: not even "existence" holds → "doesn't exist at all."

meaning: Strengthens a negative: “not at all, never” (〜やしない・〜はしない), with strong conviction, dissatisfaction or disdain, and a very colloquial feel; there are also set forms 「〜やしないか」 (“I worry it might...”) and 「〜ったらありゃしない」 (“it's unbelievably ...”).
connection: Verb ます-stem + やしない／はしない; verb te-form + やしない; verb ます-stem + やしないか; i-adjective・na-adjective + ったらありゃしない

senses.label: Definitely won't
senses.meaning: The speaker firmly states that something won't happen. Much stronger than 「〜ない」. Often used for resolve, to argue back, or to reassure someone.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + はしない / やしない (負けやしない, 忘れはしない, 逃げはしない)
examples: I will never forget you as long as I live.
I'm not going to lose over something like this.
Don't worry, nobody's going to get angry.

senses.label: Not ... at all
senses.meaning: A strong negative with annoyance, scorn, or finality. Much more emotional than 「〜ない」. Casual speech between people who know each other.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + やしない (わかりやしない, できやしない, 来やしない)
examples: No matter how long you wait, he's not going to come.
With handwriting like this, nobody can read it.
No matter how many times I tell that kid, he just doesn't listen.

senses.label: I'm afraid that ...
senses.meaning: 「〜やしないか」 expresses worry that something bad might happen, like 「〜のではないか」. Often followed by 「と心配だ」 or 「とひやひやする」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + やしないか (と心配だ)
examples: I'm worried my kid might catch a cold.
I was on edge the whole way, afraid it might rain.

senses.label: Incredibly ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ったらありゃしない」 means an extreme degree, "so ... it's unbearable," usually about something annoying. 「ありゃしない」 is a sound change of 「ありはしない」.
senses.connection: i-adjective / na-adjective + ったらありゃしない
examples: The construction next door is incredibly noisy.
The packed trains every morning are such a pain.

notes: It is very colloquial and emotional. Saying 「〜やしない」to a boss or client, or in a formal setting, sounds rude and resentful. In formal settings say 「〜ません」or 「〜のではないかと心配しております」.
「〜やしないか」means worrying that something bad "might happen"; it isn't a negation: 「落ちやしないかと心配だ」= "I'm worried it might fall." Don't read it as "it won't fall."
「〜ったらありゃしない」is mostly used for annoying things (「うるさい」, 「面倒くさい」); with good things it sounds exaggerated or teasing.
「は／や」 must follow the ます-stem (the continuative form), not the dictionary form: ✕「行くはしない」→ ○「行きはしない」. With the te-form it is 「〜てやしない」 (「聞いてやしない」 = not listening at all).
「〜はしないが」 often expresses partial negation or contrast: 「笑いはしなかったが、内心驚いた」 means “I didn't laugh, but...”. It is not a stronger negation, so do not translate it as “never laughed”.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: Mom complains her kid never listens.
daily.example: No matter how many times I tell him, he doesn't listen at all.

daily.title: Worried about a trip
daily.description: Family members worry about the weather before a trip.
daily.example: I'm worried a typhoon might come.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend in midsummer.
daily.example: This summer is unbearably hot.

daily.title: Reassuring a friend
daily.description: Your friend is worried about being blamed, and you say it'll be fine.
daily.example: It's fine. Nobody's going to hate you over something like that.

daily.title: Showing determination
daily.description: Words to yourself or your teammates before a match.
daily.example: I won't give up until the very end.

work.title: Grumbling with a coworker
work.description: A coworker complains the system is hard to use. Only among close colleagues.
work.example: This system is such a pain to use.

work.title: Grumbling with a coworker
work.description: A coworker privately complains that the boss never reads reports. Only between people who are close.
work.example: The department head never reads the reports anyway.

work.title: Reading a novel
work.description: A character in a novel makes a vow. In writing it is often 「〜はしない」.
work.example: I will never forget the humiliation of that day.

etymology: Made of the verb ます-stem + the topic particle 「は」 + 「しない」; 「は」 singles out the action and negates it, which strengthens the negation. In speech 「は」 (wa) merges with the preceding vowel and shifts to 「や」, giving 「〜やしない」; 「ありゃしない」 is likewise a contraction of 「ありはしない」.
formation: Built from verb ます-stem (continuative form) + the topic particle 「は」 + 「しない」. To negate an action one could simply say 「行かない」; here the verb is first made into its continuative form, lifted out like a noun and highlighted with 「は」, and then the whole is negated with 「しない」, the negative of 「する」: “‘going’? — that I don't do.” Because the negated action is pulled out on its own, the negation is heavier, which lets it express resolve (「忘れはしない」) or flat denial. In speech 「は」 (wa) runs into the preceding vowel and shifts to 「や」, giving 「〜やしない」; this sound-changed form is more casual and therefore often carries dissatisfaction or disdain (「聞いてやしない」). Adding 「か」 gives “might it be that...?” (「〜やしないか」), i.e. worry; 「ありはしない」 → 「ありゃしない」 after 「〜ったら」 means “speaking of ..., nothing is more ... than this”, giving “unbelievably ...”. Since 「は」 itself contrasts, 「〜はしないが」 can also mean a partial negation, “I didn't ..., but ...”. So all these senses come from the one structure of “lift the action out, then negate it”.

similar.title: 〜っこない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both are strong colloquial negations. 「〜っこない」only means "no way" (「できっこない」). 「〜やしない」can also express dissatisfaction that someone "doesn't do it at all."

similar.title: 〜もしない (not even ...)
similar.explanation: Same structure (both are masu-stem + particle + 「しない」). 「〜もしない」stresses "not even ...". 「〜やしない」comes from a sound change of 「は」and stresses "not at all."

similar.title: 〜といったらない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 「〜ったらありゃしない」; both express an extreme degree. 「〜といったらない」can be used for good things and is more formal. 「〜ったらありゃしない」is colloquial and mostly used to complain.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express resolve or flat denial. 「〜ものか」 uses a rhetorical question and is more emotional (「負けるものか」); 「〜はしない」 is a direct negation and sounds calmer.

meaning: "Whatever ... may be": sets one factor aside and then states a judgment or attitude it doesn't affect.
connection: Noun + はどうあれ／がどうあれ

senses.label: Whatever the reason
senses.meaning: Sets aside the reason, motive, or process, then gives the speaker's criticism or judgment. Common: 「理由はどうあれ」, 「事情はどうあれ」, 「動機はどうあれ」.
senses.connection: 理由／事情／動機／経緯 + はどうあれ
examples: Whatever the reason, violence is unacceptable.
Whatever the circumstances, you're the one who broke the promise.

senses.label: Whatever the result
senses.meaning: Regardless of the result, the form, or others' opinions, the speaker gives a positive view, resolve, or evaluation. Common: 「結果はどうあれ」, 「形はどうあれ」.
senses.connection: 結果／形／周り + はどうあれ／がどうあれ
examples: Whatever the result, you did great sticking with it to the end.
Whatever others think of me, I'll go my own way.
Whatever form it takes, it's enough if your feelings come across.

notes: The main clause must be the speaker's judgment, claim, or resolve; stating objective fact sounds unnatural: ✕「結果はどうあれ、試合は3時に終わった」→ ○「結果はどうあれ、全力を尽くそう」.
「理由はどうあれ」is often used to assign blame, so it sounds unsympathetic when said to a client or boss. Used in your own apology (「理由はどうあれ、ご迷惑をおかけしたのは事実です」), however, it is entirely appropriate.
Don't confuse it with 「どうあっても」("no matter what, I will"): 「どうあっても行く」expresses resolve. 「〜はどうあれ」sets the preceding factor aside, and is always preceded by 「noun + は/が」.

daily.title: Breaking up a kids' fight
daily.description: A parent speaks to children who were fighting.
daily.example: Whatever the reason, whoever hit first is in the wrong.

daily.title: Encouraging a test-taker
daily.description: After an exam, family members comfort the child.
daily.example: Whatever the result, you did really well.

work.title: Handling a complaint
work.description: A manager stresses to the team that apologizing comes first.
work.example: Whatever happened, we should first apologize to the customer.

work.title: News commentary
work.example: Whatever the motives, the direction of the reform deserves credit.

etymology: Made from the adverb 「どう」 ("how") and 「あれ」, the classical imperative of 「ある」, originally meaning "however it may be." The imperative here expresses concession, the same idea as 「何はともあれ」 and 「いずれにせよ」.

similar.title: 〜はともかく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜はともかく」means "setting ... aside for now," implying something more important comes next. 「〜はどうあれ」stresses that "however ... may be, it doesn't affect the judgment that follows."

similar.title: 〜であれ／〜であれ〜であれ
similar.explanation: Same origin (both use the imperative 「あれ」of 「ある」to concede). 「〜であれ」takes a concrete noun or question word (「誰であれ」, 「何であれ」). 「〜はどうあれ」takes abstract nouns such as 「理由」and 「結果」.

similar.title: 〜いかんにかかわらず／〜いかんを問わず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜いかんにかかわらず」is more formal, mostly for rules and official documents. 「〜はどうあれ」is better suited to expressing the speaker's own attitude.

similar.title: 〜にしろ・〜にせよ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express concession. 「〜にしろ」can follow various clauses. 「〜はどうあれ」is the fixed pattern 「noun + はどうあれ」.

formation: It is 「どう」("how") + the classical imperative 「あれ」of 「ある」. The imperative here isn't a command but a "let it be" permissiveness: "(the reason) can be whatever." You set the preceding factor aside, concede it can be anything, then state the main clause, so the main clause is necessarily a judgment or attitude unaffected by it. 「であれ」and 「であろうと」also use the imperative and volitional of 「ある」to concede, which is why they are interchangeable.
